rv.q: About 15 minutes into the antics of this most loathsome trio — talk about a play with no one to like — I started staring down at the program in the hope that we might at least be seeing another character with the potential to relieve us from this trio.
Overall, FAULT is enjoyable and full of Jerry and Lucy's increasingly ridiculous antics — even if at a certain point you just want to tell them to enjoy all their money and stop fighting.
'Fault' has mild amusements and noble performances, but it's stuck in a low comic gear that shifts tones without ever finding an authentic one.

And just when the night seems like it can't twist any further, the play barrels into a smash bang ending that lands with real force - the kind that sends audiences out buzzing, debating, and replaying the final moments long after the curtain comes down.
Rebecca Spence is a standout. She's simply brilliant.
Together, they form a perfect example of a dynamic partnership, creating a foundation for a masterclass in theater that showcases storytelling at its finest.
If you miss this entertaining play you will have to fly somewhere to see it– save yourself a trip!

At the start, we see the always-excellent Rebecca Spence as Lucy in a high-rise living room with a boy toy she met at a bar earlier in the evening. We've caught the two of them at the start of a sexual encounter…and we're not the only ones. Almost immediately, Lucy's husband Jerry, played by Enrico Colantoni, walks in and interrupts their liaison.
It’s a diverting example of the genre with a luxe production handsomely designed by Paul Tate Depoo III, with a mix of designer taste and Billionaire’s Row gauche.
Although FAULT tries for darkly comic autopsy of a marriage, it never gets too vicious or absurd.

But though it's only 90 minutes long, nearly every moment of this show felt so preordained and predictable that, even with Chicago stalwart Rebecca Spence killing it in a role originally planned for Teri Hatcher (who left the cast for unknown reasons), it feels like a slog.
Unpleasant, unfunny, misogynistic, and worst of all, boring.
The entire production is one that they can be proud of, and you will enjoy from start to finish.
